title: Nathrop Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Nathrop wells have a 100 ft median depth, 12 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $12,500-$22,000.
h1: Nathrop Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Nathrop means dealing mostly with mountain bedrock, not a uniform shallow valley aquifer. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a median total depth of 100 feet, but actual results vary substantially. The middle half runs from 59 to 200 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 840 feet.

Yield records are generally favorable, with a 12.0 gallons-per-minute median among wells reporting a pump yield. Those figures are useful for comparing a property with its neighbors, but they are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. A site-specific driller’s review, permit check, septic layout, and water-quality testing still matter.

sections.heading: Nathrop well depth is usually shallow, but bedrock controls the bid
sections.html:
The local depth median is 100 feet, and 47% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Another 39% fall between 100 and 300 feet. That makes a standard drilling estimate possible, but not certain: 13% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 840 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 1,220 wells, compared with 39 alluvial wells and 1 Quaternary Alluvium well. In granite and gneiss, water commonly depends on fractures, so two nearby lots can drill very differently. For a bid, the 59-to-200-foot middle half is more useful than the median alone. Ask what happens to the price if the hole must continue toward the local 90th-percentile depth of 321 feet.

sections.heading: What Nathrop wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 499 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. The records show 74% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 5% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a solid local record for domestic wells, but a pump-yield entry is not the same as an unlimited supply. A buyer should ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage setup, and any production limitations. Household use is the main permit purpose at 80%; stock use is 10%, monitoring is 10%, and irrigation is 1%, so irrigation expectations require separate review.

sections.heading: Nathrop water levels and the decade comparison
sections.html:
Only 192 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is smaller than the depth and yield record. The median static water level is 68 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 44 to 162 feet. That tells you where water stood when those wells were measured, not necessarily the level during pumping or a dry season.

The decade comparison shows a higher median depth to water in the 2020s than in the 2010s: 76 feet below surface versus 58 feet. That change suggests the measured wells had deeper water levels in the newer decade, but it does not by itself prove a region-wide declining water table. Measurement dates, locations, well construction, and pumping conditions matter. Have a driller compare nearby records rather than relying on a countywide assumption.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady drilling around Nathrop
sections.html:
There are 1,271 permitted wells in the records for the area, with 845 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was limited in the 1950s and 1960s, with 17 and 9 permits respectively, then increased to 83 in both the 1970s and 1980s. The 1990s show 256 permits, followed by 288 in the 2000s, 158 in the 2010s, and 180 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most active names in the records are American Drilling Service, associated with Dewberry, Bradford W., with 184 wells; Whitewater Systems, Inc., associated with Shake, Shawn, with 128; and Mccoy Drilling Inc, associated with Dennison, Lynn A., with 126. These counts describe permit history, not a performance ranking. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring anyone.

sections.heading: Nathrop well drilling cost: plan for the full installation
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite or gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500 to $10,000. That is only the hole, not a working water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move outside that range, especially if casing, grout, access, difficult setup, or additional electrical work is needed. Get the bid in writing and identify the included depth, casing and grout, pump size, testing, trenching distance, power connection, and the price per additional foot.

sections.heading: What to investigate before building near Nathrop
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk are the main technical concerns in fractured bedrock, even though the reported yield distribution is favorable. The records also map 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 527 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped sites do not automatically make a particular well unsafe, but they justify a location-specific water test and a review of nearby land uses.

Check the well permit and construction record through Colorado DWR, then test for bacteria, basic chemistry, and contaminants appropriate to the property history. Confirm setbacks between the well, septic system, leach field, fuel storage, mines, and surface water. Before closing, make sure the proposed home, driveway, drilling rig access, septic design, and electrical route can all fit on the lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Nathrop, Colorado?
faq.a: Nathrop wells in the records have a median depth of 100 feet. The middle half runs from 59 to 200 feet, while 47% are under 100 feet. Conditions vary because 1,220 permits name fractured bedrock, and recorded depths range as far as 840 feet. Nearby wells help set expectations, but they cannot guarantee a new hole.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Nathrop?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured granite or gneiss. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500 to $10,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Nathrop wells produce?
faq.a: Among 499 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Records show 74% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 21% above 15, and 5% between 1 and 5. These are local records, not a promise for an un drilled lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Nathrop, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its surroundings. The area includes 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 527 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test a new or transferred well for bacteria and chemistry, and add testing based on mining or other nearby land-use concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Nathrop?
faq.a: The available static-water sample includes 192 wells. Its median depth to water was 58 feet below surface in the 2010s and 76 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured level in the newer decade, but the series alone does not prove a regional decline. Well location, measurement conditions, construction, and pumping history should be reviewed.
